subject: hge
title: Hydraulics and Principles of Geotechnical Engineering

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Gauge pressure under two immiscible liquid layers
questions.stem: An open tank contains a 2.5 m layer of oil ($SG = 0.85$) floating on 1.5 m of water. What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
given: Tank open to the atmosphere (gauge pressure zero at the surface)
questions.required: The gauge pressure $p$ at the bottom of the tank.

variables.meaning: Gauge pressure at the tank bottom

solution.title: Pressure from the oil layer
solution.text: Multiply the oil unit weight by its thickness.

solution.title: Pressure from the water layer
solution.text: The water layer adds its own $\gamma h$ on top of the oil contribution.

solution.title: Sum the layers
solution.text: Gauge pressure at the bottom is the sum of the layer contributions.

questions.insight: Pressure accumulates layer by layer; each layer contributes its own unit weight times its own thickness, regardless of what lies above it.
commonErrors: Treating the full 4.0 m as water gives 39.24 kPa.
Swapping the layer thicknesses (oil 1.5 m, water 2.5 m) gives 37.03 kPa.
Treating the full 4.0 m as oil gives 33.35 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Open U-tube mercury manometer on a water pipe
questions.stem: A pipe carrying water is connected to an open U-tube mercury manometer ($SG = 13.6$). The centre of the pipe, point A, is 0.40 m above the mercury surface in the leg attached to the pipe. The mercury in the open leg stands 0.25 m above the mercury surface in the pipe leg. Find the gauge pressure at A. Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
given: Water column from A down to the mercury surface: $0.40\text{ m}$
questions.required: The gauge pressure $p_A$ at the pipe centre.

variables.meaning: Gauge pressure at the pipe centre

solution.title: Write the manometer equation
solution.text: Start at A, go down 0.40 m of water, then up 0.25 m of mercury to the open end (gauge pressure zero).

solution.title: Evaluate the columns
solution.text: Compute each column's pressure.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Solve for the gauge pressure at A.

questions.insight: Going down a column adds pressure and going up subtracts it; the light water column partly offsets the heavy mercury column.
commonErrors: Ignoring the 0.40 m water column gives 33.35 kPa.
Adding the water column instead of subtracting it (sign error) gives 37.28 kPa.
Treating the whole 0.65 m as mercury gives 86.72 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Total force on a vertical rectangular gate
questions.stem: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high holds back water. Its top edge is 1.5 m below the water surface. What is the total hydrostatic force on the gate? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
questions.required: The total hydrostatic force $F$ on the gate.

variables.meaning: Depth of the centroid of the gate

solution.title: Depth of the centroid
solution.text: The centroid of a rectangle is at mid-height.

solution.title: Area of the gate
solution.text: Width times height.

solution.title: Total force
solution.text: Apply $F = \gamma \bar{h} A$.

questions.insight: The resultant equals the pressure at the centroid times the area; its line of action (center of pressure) lies lower, at 3.25 m depth.
commonErrors: Using the depth of the top edge (1.5 m) gives 88.29 kN.
Using the depth of the center of pressure (3.25 m) instead of the centroid gives 191.30 kN.
Using the depth of the bottom edge (4.5 m) gives 264.87 kN.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Force to hold a hinged inclined gate closed
questions.stem: A rectangular gate 1.5 m wide and 2.4 m long (measured along its slope) is inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal and holds back water on one side. It is hinged along its top edge, which is 1.2 m vertically below the water surface. What force, applied normal to the gate at its bottom edge, is needed to keep it closed? Neglect the weight of the gate and use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
given: Gate width $b = 1.5\text{ m}$, inclined length $L = 2.4\text{ m}$
Vertical depth of hinge (top edge) $= 1.2\text{ m}$
questions.required: The normal force $P$ at the bottom edge that keeps the gate closed.

variables.meaning: Inclined distance from the free-surface line to the centroid
Distance from centroid to center of pressure along the gate
Centroidal moment of inertia of the gate
Required normal force at the bottom edge

solution.title: Locate the centroid
solution.text: Measure distances along the incline from the line where the gate plane meets the free surface.

solution.title: Resultant force
solution.text: The vertical depth of the centroid is $\bar{y}\sin\theta$.

solution.title: Eccentricity of the center of pressure
solution.text: Use the centroidal moment of inertia of the rectangle.

solution.title: Moments about the hinge
solution.text: The arm of $F$ from the hinge is $1.2 + e$; the arm of $P$ is the full 2.4 m.

questions.insight: The center of pressure is always below the centroid, so the hinge carries less than half the resultant and the bottom support carries more than half.
commonErrors: Placing F at the centroid (ignoring e) gives F/2 = 39.54 kN.
Taking the centroid depth as $1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4$ m vertically (forgetting to resolve the inclined length by $\sin 60^\circ$) gives $F = 84.76$ kN and $P = 48.50$ kN.
Using $\cos 60^\circ$ instead of $\sin 60^\circ$ for an angle measured from the horizontal gives 35.32 kN.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Velocity in a contracted pipe by continuity
questions.stem: Water flows through a pipe that reduces from 300 mm to 150 mm in diameter. The velocity in the 300 mm section is 1.2 m/s. What is the velocity in the 150 mm section?
questions.required: The mean velocity $V_2$ in the 150 mm section.

formulas.label: Continuity (incompressible flow)
formulas.tex: Q = A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 \;\Rightarrow\; V_2 = V_1\left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2

variables.meaning: Mean velocities in the large and small sections

solution.title: Write continuity
solution.text: For circular pipes the area ratio is the square of the diameter ratio.

solution.title: Substitute
solution.text: Use the given diameters and velocity.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute the velocity.

questions.insight: Halving the diameter quarters the area, so the velocity quadruples for the same discharge.
commonErrors: Using the diameter ratio without squaring gives 2.40 m/s.
Inverting the ratio (thinking velocity drops in the smaller pipe) gives 0.30 m/s.
Cubing the diameter ratio gives 9.60 m/s.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Pressure drop at a horizontal pipe contraction
questions.stem: A horizontal pipe reduces from 300 mm to 150 mm in diameter and carries water at $0.10\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$. The pressure in the 300 mm section is 150 kPa. Neglecting losses, what is the pressure in the 150 mm section? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
questions.required: The pressure $p_2$ in the 150 mm section.

variables.meaning: Pressures in the large and small sections

solution.title: Velocities from continuity
solution.text: Divide the discharge by each area.

solution.title: Bernoulli with equal elevations
solution.text: The elevation terms cancel.

solution.title: Change in velocity head
solution.text: Compute the gain in velocity head.

solution.title: Convert to pressure
solution.text: Multiply the head by $\gamma_w$ and subtract.

questions.insight: Velocity increases at the contraction, so the pressure must drop by the gain in velocity head; this is the principle of the venturi meter.
commonErrors: Adding the velocity-head change instead of subtracting it gives 165.01 kPa.
Ignoring the upstream velocity head $V_1^2/2g$ gives 133.99 kPa.
Subtracting the velocity-head change in metres directly from kPa (no conversion) gives 148.47 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Darcy-Weisbach head loss in a long pipe
questions.stem: Water flows at $0.06\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ through an 800 m long, 250 mm diameter pipe with friction factor $f = 0.02$. What is the head loss due to friction? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.

solution.title: Mean velocity
solution.text: From continuity.

solution.title: Darcy-Weisbach
solution.text: Substitute into the head-loss equation.

solution.title: Check with the discharge form
solution.text: The $Q$-form gives the same result.

questions.insight: Friction loss varies with $Q^2/D^5$, so a modest increase in diameter drastically reduces head loss.
commonErrors: Dropping the 2 in $2g$ doubles the answer to 9.75 m.
Using V instead of V² gives 3.99 m.
Using $A = \pi D^2$ (omitting the 1/4) for the velocity gives 0.30 m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Discharge from a reservoir through a free-discharging pipe
questions.stem: A 300 mm pipe, 400 m long, draws water from a reservoir and discharges freely into the air at a point 30 m below the reservoir water surface. Take $f = 0.02$, $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ and neglect minor losses. What is the discharge?
given: Free jet at the outlet; minor losses neglected

variables.meaning: Elevation difference between reservoir surface and outlet

solution.title: Energy equation
solution.text: From the reservoir surface (1) to the free jet (2): $p_1 = p_2 = 0$ and $V_1 = 0$.

solution.title: Solve for velocity
solution.text: Rearrange for $V$.

solution.title: Discharge
solution.text: Multiply by the pipe area.

questions.insight: The available head is split between the exit velocity head and friction; for a long pipe friction dominates, but the exit head is not negligible.
commonErrors: Omitting the exit velocity head (setting $30 = h_f$ only) gives $0.332\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Using $A = \pi D^2$ instead of $\pi D^2/4$ gives $1.304\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Ignoring friction entirely ($V = \sqrt{2gH}$) gives $1.715\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Porosity from void ratio
questions.stem: A soil has a void ratio of 0.65. What is its porosity?

solution.title: Recall the definitions
solution.text: Taking $V_s = 1$, the voids occupy $e$ and the total volume is $1 + e$.

solution.title: Substitute
solution.text: Use the given void ratio.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute.

questions.insight: Porosity is always less than 1, while void ratio can exceed 1 in loose or highly plastic soils.
commonErrors: Computing $1/(1+e)$, which is the solids fraction $V_s/V$, gives 0.606.
Using $e/(1-e)$ gives 1.857, which is impossible since $n < 1$.
Confusing porosity with void ratio gives 0.650.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Moist unit weight from w, Gs and S
questions.stem: A soil has water content $w = 18\%$, specific gravity of solids $G_s = 2.70$, and degree of saturation $S = 80\%$. What is its moist unit weight? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.

solution.title: Void ratio
solution.text: Use $Se = wG_s$.

solution.title: Moist unit weight formula
solution.text: Substitute into the moist unit weight expression.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute.

questions.insight: Always get the void ratio first; once $e$ is known every unit weight follows from one formula with the appropriate $S$.
commonErrors: Computing the dry unit weight $G_s\gamma_w/(1+e)$ gives 16.48.
Using $S = 1$ in the numerator (saturated unit weight) gives 20.18.
Assuming saturation so that $e = wG_s = 0.486$ gives 21.03.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Degree of saturation from a field density test
questions.stem: A field density test gives a moist unit weight of $18.5\text{ kN/m}^3$ and a water content of 15%. The specific gravity of solids is 2.68. What is the degree of saturation? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.

solution.title: Dry unit weight
solution.text: Remove the water from the moist unit weight.

solution.title: Void ratio
solution.text: From the dry unit weight relation.

solution.title: Degree of saturation
solution.text: Apply $Se = wG_s$.

questions.insight: The relation $e = G_s\gamma_w/\gamma_d - 1$ is only valid with the dry unit weight; using the moist value grossly overstates saturation.
commonErrors: Using the moist unit weight in $e = G_s\gamma_w/\gamma - 1$ gives $e = 0.421$ and $S = 95.5\%$.
Using $\gamma_d = \gamma(1 - w)$ gives $S = 59.8\%$.
Using $\gamma_w = 10\text{ kN/m}^3$ gives $S = 60.4\%$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Effective stress in a sand-over-clay profile
questions.stem: A soil profile has 3 m of sand ($\gamma = 17\text{ kN/m}^3$) over clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 19\text{ kN/m}^3$). The water table is at the top of the clay. What is the effective vertical stress at a depth of 8 m below the ground surface? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
given: Water table at 3 m depth (top of clay)
Point of interest at 8 m depth
questions.required: The effective vertical stress $\sigma'$ at 8 m depth.

solution.title: Total stress at 8 m
solution.text: Sum the unit weight times thickness of each layer.

solution.title: Pore pressure
solution.text: The point is 5 m below the water table.

solution.title: Effective stress
solution.text: Subtract the pore pressure.

questions.insight: Pore pressure is measured from the water table, not from the ground surface.
commonErrors: Reporting the total stress (146.00 kPa) instead of the effective stress.
Measuring pore pressure from the ground surface instead of the water table gives 67.52 kPa.
Reporting the pore pressure (49.05 kPa) instead of the effective stress.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Change in effective stress after lowering the water table
questions.stem: The water table in a uniform soil is initially at the ground surface. The soil has $\gamma_{sat} = 19.5\text{ kN/m}^3$, and its moist unit weight when above the water table is $17.5\text{ kN/m}^3$. If the water table is lowered permanently to 2 m below the surface, by how much does the effective stress at a depth of 6 m change? Take an increase as positive and use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
given: $\gamma_{sat} = 19.5\text{ kN/m}^3$, $\gamma = 17.5\text{ kN/m}^3$ above the water table
Water table lowered from the surface to 2 m depth
Point of interest at 6 m depth
questions.required: The change in effective stress $\Delta\sigma'$ at 6 m depth.

formulas.label: Effective stress with submerged unit weight

solution.title: Initial effective stress
solution.text: The whole 6 m is submerged.

solution.title: Final effective stress
solution.text: 2 m of moist soil above 4 m of submerged soil.

solution.title: Change
solution.text: Subtract the initial from the final value.

questions.insight: Lowering the water table increases effective stress, which is why groundwater pumping can trigger settlement of soft deposits.
commonErrors: Assuming only the pore pressure changes ($2\gamma_w$) and ignoring the drop from $\gamma_{sat}$ to $\gamma$ gives 19.62 kPa.
Reporting the final effective stress (73.76 kPa) instead of the change.
Reporting the initial effective stress as a decrease (58.14 kPa) confuses the stress state with the change.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Friction angle from a drained triaxial test
questions.stem: A consolidated-drained triaxial test on a normally consolidated clay ($c' = 0$) is run at a cell pressure of 100 kPa. Failure occurs at a deviator stress of 180 kPa. What is the effective angle of internal friction?

formulas.label: Mohr circle tangent to an envelope through the origin

variables.meaning: Major and minor principal stresses at failure

solution.title: Major principal stress
solution.text: Add the deviator stress to the cell pressure.

solution.title: Geometry of the Mohr circle
solution.text: With $c' = 0$ the envelope passes through the origin.

solution.title: Friction angle
solution.text: Take the inverse sine.

questions.insight: For a cohesionless envelope the ratio of circle radius to centre distance equals $\sin\phi'$.
commonErrors: Using $\tan^{-1}$ instead of $\sin^{-1}$ gives $25.35^\circ$.
Using $(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/\sigma_1$ gives $40.01^\circ$.
Taking the deviator stress as $\sigma_1$ (180 kPa) gives $16.60^\circ$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Primary consolidation settlement of an NC clay under fill
questions.stem: A profile consists of 5 m of sand over a 4 m layer of normally consolidated clay. The water table is 2 m below the ground surface. Sand: $\gamma = 17\text{ kN/m}^3$ above the water table, $\gamma_{sat} = 19\text{ kN/m}^3$ below. Clay: $\gamma_{sat} = 18.5\text{ kN/m}^3$, $e_0 = 1.10$, $C_c = 0.35$. A wide fill adds a uniform 60 kPa at the clay. Estimate the primary consolidation settlement of the clay using the stress at mid-depth of the clay and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.

variables.meaning: Initial effective stress at mid-depth of the clay

solution.title: Initial effective stress at mid-clay (7 m depth)
solution.text: Use moist weight above the water table and submerged weights below.

solution.title: Final effective stress
solution.text: Add the fill stress.

solution.title: Settlement
solution.text: Apply the NC consolidation equation.

solution.title: Convert
solution.text: Express in millimetres.

questions.insight: Consolidation is driven by effective stress; a lower initial effective stress makes the same load produce a larger settlement.
commonErrors: Using total stress (128 kPa) instead of effective stress gives 111.3 mm.
Dividing by $e_0$ instead of $1 + e_0$ gives 312.5 mm.
Using $\ln$ instead of $\log_{10}$ gives 376.9 mm.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Capillary rise of water in a glass tube
questions.stem: A clean glass tube with an internal diameter of 2.0 mm is inserted vertically into water. The surface tension of water is $\sigma = 0.0728\text{ N/m}$ and the contact angle is $0^\circ$. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, how high will the water rise in the tube above the outside water surface?

formulas.label: Capillary rise in a circular tube

solution.title: Balance surface tension and weight
solution.text: The vertical surface-tension force around the perimeter supports the raised column: $\sigma\cos\theta(\pi d) = \gamma h(\pi d^2/4)$.

solution.title: Substitute in consistent units
solution.text: Use newtons and metres.

solution.title: Compute
solution.text: Evaluate and convert to millimetres.

questions.insight: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to tube diameter, which is why fine-grained soils with tiny pores show large capillary heights.
commonErrors: Using the radius (1 mm) in place of the diameter in $4\sigma/(\gamma d)$ gives 29.68 mm.
Using $2\sigma/(\gamma d)$ (a radius formula with the diameter) gives 7.42 mm.
Using the density 1000 kg/m³ instead of the unit weight 9810 N/m³ gives 145.6 mm.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Kinematic viscosity of a lubricating oil
questions.stem: A lubricating oil has a dynamic viscosity of $0.048\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ and a specific gravity of 0.92. Taking the density of water as $1000\text{ kg/m}^3$, what is the kinematic viscosity of the oil in centistokes ($1\text{ cSt} = 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$)?

solution.title: Density of the oil
solution.text: Multiply the specific gravity by the density of water.

solution.title: Kinematic viscosity
solution.text: Divide the dynamic viscosity by the density.

solution.title: Convert to centistokes
solution.text: Divide by $10^{-6}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$ per cSt.

questions.insight: Kinematic viscosity combines viscous and inertial properties and is the quantity that enters the Reynolds number $VD/\nu$.
commonErrors: Using the density of water (1000 kg/m³) instead of the oil gives 48.00 cSt.
Multiplying by the specific gravity instead of dividing gives 44.16 cSt.
Converting with stokes ($10^{-4}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$) instead of centistokes gives 0.52.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Terminal velocity of a plate sliding on an oil film
questions.stem: A flat plate 0.50 m by 0.80 m weighing 120 N slides down a plane inclined at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal. The plate is separated from the plane by an oil film 1.2 mm thick with dynamic viscosity $\mu = 0.15\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$. Assuming a linear velocity profile in the film, what is the terminal (steady) velocity of the plate?
questions.required: The terminal velocity $V$ of the plate.

solution.title: Driving force
solution.text: Only the component of weight parallel to the incline drives the plate.

solution.title: Viscous resisting force
solution.text: With a linear profile the shear stress is uniform.

solution.title: Set forces equal at terminal velocity
solution.text: Solve for $V$.

questions.insight: At terminal velocity the viscous drag exactly balances the gravity component; a thinner film or more viscous oil slows the plate proportionally.
commonErrors: Using $\cos 20^\circ$ for the driving component gives 2.255 m/s.
Using the full weight as the driving force gives 2.400 m/s.
Using $\tan 20^\circ$ instead of $\sin 20^\circ$ gives 0.874 m/s.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Resultant force on a quarter-circle gate
questions.stem: A gate in the shape of a quarter-cylinder of radius 2.0 m and length 3.0 m (perpendicular to the page) forms the lower corner of a water tank. Its vertical projection is 2.0 m high and the water surface is level with the top edge of the gate. The water lying vertically above the curved surface occupies exactly the quarter-circle region of the cross-section. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, find the magnitude of the resultant hydrostatic force on the gate.
given: Water surface level with the top of the gate
Water above the curved surface fills the quarter-circle region
questions.required: The magnitude of the resultant hydrostatic force $F$.

solution.title: Horizontal component
solution.text: The vertical projection is a 2.0 m by 3.0 m rectangle with centroid 1.0 m deep.

solution.title: Vertical component
solution.text: Weight of the quarter-circle volume of water above the gate.

solution.title: Resultant
solution.text: Combine the perpendicular components.

questions.insight: For a circular gate every pressure force is normal to the surface, so the resultant passes through the centre of curvature; here it acts at about $57.5^\circ$ below the horizontal.
commonErrors: Adding the components arithmetically instead of vectorially gives 151.32 kN.
Using the full 2 m by 2 m square of water instead of the quarter circle for $F_V$ gives 131.62 kN.
Reporting only the vertical component gives 92.46 kN.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Apparent weight of a stone submerged in oil
questions.stem: A stone weighs 420 N in air and 260 N when fully submerged in water. What will it weigh when fully submerged in an oil of specific gravity 0.82? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.
questions.required: The apparent weight of the stone in oil.

solution.title: Buoyant force in water
solution.text: The loss of weight in water equals the buoyant force.

solution.title: Buoyant force in oil
solution.text: The displaced volume is the same, so the buoyant force scales with the specific gravity of the fluid.

solution.title: Apparent weight in oil
solution.text: Subtract the oil buoyancy from the weight in air.

questions.insight: The stone's volume is $160/9810 = 0.0163\text{ m}^3$ and its specific gravity is $420/160 = 2.625$; a lighter fluid buoys it less.
commonErrors: Multiplying the weight in water by 0.82 gives 213.2 N.
Dividing the water buoyancy by 0.82 instead of multiplying gives 224.9 N.
Dividing the weight in water by 0.82 gives 317.1 N.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Righting moment of a heeled rectangular barge
questions.stem: A rectangular barge 12 m long and 6 m wide weighs 1400 kN and floats in fresh water ($\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$). Its centre of gravity is 1.80 m above the bottom. Compute the righting moment when the barge heels by $4^\circ$ about its longitudinal axis, using the small-angle metacentric formula $M = W\,GM\sin\theta$.

variables.meaning: Height of centre of buoyancy above the keel

solution.title: Draft
solution.text: The displaced water weighs the same as the barge.

solution.title: Centre of buoyancy
solution.text: For a rectangular hull it is at half the draft.

solution.title: Metacentric radius
solution.text: Rolling about the longitudinal axis uses the width cubed.

solution.title: Metacentric height
solution.text: Combine the vertical distances.

solution.title: Righting moment
solution.text: Apply the small-angle formula.

questions.insight: A positive $GM$ means the metacentre lies above G and the barge is stable; the wide beam (B cubed in $I$) is what gives a barge its stability.
commonErrors: Using the length instead of the width in $I$ ($BM = L^2/12D$) gives 512.24 kN·m.
Forgetting the centre of buoyancy ($GM = BM - KG$) gives a negative moment of -27.98 kN·m.
Taking $KB$ as the full draft instead of half gives 165.60 kN·m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Maximum speed of a rotating open cylinder
questions.stem: An open cylindrical tank 0.80 m in diameter and 1.50 m high contains water to a depth of 1.10 m. The tank is rotated about its vertical axis. At what speed, in revolutions per minute, will water just begin to spill over the rim? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.required: The rotational speed $N$ (rpm) at which spilling begins.

formulas.label: Volume of a paraboloid
formulas.tex: V_{par} = \tfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2 h \;\Rightarrow\; \text{rise at wall} = \text{drop at centre} = \tfrac{h}{2}

variables.meaning: Height of the paraboloid (rim to vertex)

solution.title: Paraboloid height
solution.text: Since no water is lost and the vertex stays above the bottom, the surface rises $h/2$ at the wall. Spilling starts when the wall level reaches the rim.

solution.title: Check the vertex
solution.text: The vertex is at $1.10 - 0.40 = 0.70\text{ m}$ above the bottom, so the bottom is not exposed and the relation holds.

solution.title: Angular speed
solution.text: Solve the paraboloid equation for $\omega$.

solution.title: Convert to rpm
solution.text: Multiply by $60/2\pi$.

questions.insight: The free surface rises at the wall by exactly as much as it falls at the axis, because a paraboloid occupies half the volume of its circumscribing cylinder.
commonErrors: Taking the paraboloid height as only 0.40 m (forgetting the volume relation) gives 66.88 rpm.
Using the diameter as the radius gives 47.29 rpm.
Reporting the angular speed in rad/s (9.90) as rpm.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Factor of safety against overturning of a gravity dam
questions.stem: A concrete gravity dam has a vertical upstream face, a top width of 2 m, a base width of 8 m and a height of 12 m; the downstream face slopes uniformly from the top downstream corner to the toe. Water stands 11 m deep against the upstream face and there is no tailwater. Uplift pressure varies linearly from full hydrostatic head at the heel to zero at the toe and acts over the whole base. Using $\gamma_c = 23.5\text{ kN/m}^3$ and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, compute the factor of safety against overturning about the toe, per metre length of dam.
given: Top width $2\text{ m}$, base width $8\text{ m}$, height $12\text{ m}$, vertical upstream face
Upstream water depth $h = 11\text{ m}$, no tailwater
Uplift: triangular, full head at heel to zero at toe
questions.required: The factor of safety against overturning $FS_{OT}$.

formulas.label: Uplift
formulas.tex: U = \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma_w h B \text{ acting at } \tfrac{2}{3}B \text{ from the toe}

variables.meaning: Weights of the rectangular and triangular parts of the dam
Resisting and overturning moments about the toe

solution.title: Weights and arms about the toe
solution.text: Split the section into a 2 m by 12 m rectangle (centroid 7 m from the toe) and a triangle of base 6 m (centroid 4 m from the toe).

solution.title: Resisting moment
solution.text: Sum the weight moments about the toe.

solution.title: Water thrust moment
solution.text: The thrust acts at one third of the depth above the base.

solution.title: Uplift moment
solution.text: The uplift triangle has its resultant at $2B/3 = 5.333\text{ m}$ from the toe.

solution.title: Factor of safety
solution.text: Divide resisting by overturning moments.

questions.insight: Uplift contributes more overturning moment than the water thrust here, which is why drainage galleries that cut uplift are so effective in gravity dams.
commonErrors: Neglecting uplift gives 3.369.
Placing the uplift resultant at $B/3$ from the toe instead of $2B/3$ gives 2.204.
Placing the water thrust at mid-depth instead of at $h/3$ gives 1.317.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Flow division between two parallel pipes
questions.stem: Two pipes connect junctions A and B in parallel. Pipe 1: length 600 m, diameter 300 mm, $f = 0.020$. Pipe 2: length 800 m, diameter 200 mm, $f = 0.025$. The total flow from A to B is $0.20\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$. Neglecting minor losses, how much flow, in litres per second, passes through pipe 2?

solution.title: Equal head loss
solution.text: Both pipes connect the same two junctions, so $k_1Q_1^2 = k_2Q_2^2$; the constant $8/\pi^2 g$ cancels.

solution.title: Evaluate the ratio
solution.text: Substitute the pipe data.

solution.title: Apply continuity
solution.text: The two flows add to the total.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Convert to litres per second and check the head loss.
solution.tex: Q_2 = 43.88\text{ L/s} \qquad h_f \approx 9.94\text{ m in each pipe}

questions.insight: In parallel pipes flow divides so that head losses are equal; because $Q \propto D^{2.5}$, the larger pipe carries a disproportionately large share.
commonErrors: Dividing the flow in proportion to the pipe areas gives 61.54 L/s.
Forgetting the square root in the flow ratio gives 14.65 L/s.
Reporting the flow in pipe 1 (156.12 L/s) instead of pipe 2.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Discharge through a sharp-edged orifice
questions.stem: Water discharges from a large open tank through a 50 mm diameter sharp-edged orifice in its side. The water surface is maintained 4.0 m above the centre of the orifice. The coefficient of contraction is 0.62 and the coefficient of velocity is 0.98. What is the discharge in litres per second? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.

formulas.label: Orifice discharge
formulas.tex: Q = C_d A\sqrt{2gH}, \qquad C_d = C_c C_v

solution.title: Coefficient of discharge
solution.text: Multiply the two coefficients.

solution.title: Orifice area and ideal velocity
solution.text: Compute the area and the Torricelli velocity.

solution.title: Discharge
solution.text: Apply the orifice equation and convert to L/s.

questions.insight: The actual discharge is only about 61% of the ideal because the jet contracts at the vena contracta and loses a little velocity to friction.
commonErrors: Ignoring both coefficients (ideal flow) gives 17.39 L/s.
Using the diameter as the radius in the area gives 42.28 L/s.
Using $\sqrt{gH}$ instead of $\sqrt{2gH}$ gives 7.47 L/s.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Francis formula for a contracted rectangular weir
questions.stem: A sharp-crested rectangular weir 2.5 m long has end contractions at both ends. The head over the crest is 0.40 m. Neglecting velocity of approach, compute the discharge using the Francis formula $Q = 1.84\,(L - 0.1nH)\,H^{3/2}$ (SI units).

solution.title: Effective crest length
solution.text: Each end contraction reduces the effective length by $0.1H$.

solution.title: Head term
solution.text: Raise the head to the 3/2 power.

solution.title: Discharge
solution.text: Apply the Francis formula.

questions.insight: End contractions narrow the nappe; the Francis correction of $0.1H$ per contraction reduces the flow by about 3% here.
commonErrors: Ignoring the end contractions gives $1.164\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Deducting $0.2H$ per contraction gives $1.089\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Using $H$ instead of $H^{3/2}$ gives $1.781\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Force of a water jet on a fixed flat plate
questions.stem: A horizontal water jet 75 mm in diameter with a velocity of 20 m/s strikes a large fixed flat plate held perpendicular to the jet. The water leaves the plate radially in the plane of the plate. Taking $\rho = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$, what force does the jet exert on the plate?
given: Plate fixed and normal to the jet

formulas.label: Impulse-momentum (normal plate)
formulas.tex: F = \rho Q (V_1 - V_2) = \rho Q V \quad (V_2 = 0 \text{ in the jet direction})

solution.title: Jet area and discharge
solution.text: Use continuity.

solution.title: Momentum change
solution.text: The water leaves along the plate, so all momentum in the jet direction is destroyed.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Convert newtons to kilonewtons.

questions.insight: A fixed flat plate removes the jet's momentum once; a curved vane that turns the jet back would nearly double the force.
commonErrors: Using $2\rho QV$ (as for a jet fully reversed by a cup) gives 3.534 kN.
Using the diameter as the radius gives 7.069 kN.
Using $\rho A V$ (the mass flow rate) as the force gives 0.0884 kN.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Input power of a pump lifting water between reservoirs
questions.stem: A pump delivers $0.12\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ of water from a lower reservoir with water surface at elevation 100 m to an upper reservoir with water surface at elevation 145 m. The total head loss in the suction and discharge pipes is 6.5 m. If the pump efficiency is 78%, what power must be supplied to the pump? Use $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$.

variables.meaning: Total head added by the pump

solution.title: Pump head
solution.text: Between the two reservoir surfaces pressures are atmospheric and velocities zero.

solution.title: Water power
solution.text: Power delivered to the water.

solution.title: Input power
solution.text: Divide by the efficiency.

questions.insight: The pump must supply the static lift plus all pipe losses, and the motor must supply more than that because of pump inefficiency.
commonErrors: Reporting the water power (no efficiency) gives 60.63 kW.
Multiplying by the efficiency instead of dividing gives 47.29 kW.
Ignoring the pipe losses gives 67.92 kW.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Uniform flow in a trapezoidal canal by Manning
questions.stem: An irrigation canal in Nueva Ecija has a trapezoidal section with a bottom width of 3.0 m and side slopes of 1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical. It is lined with concrete ($n = 0.015$) and laid on a slope of 0.0008. Compute the discharge when water flows uniformly at a depth of 1.2 m.

formulas.label: Trapezoidal section
formulas.tex: A = (b + zy)y \qquad P = b + 2y\sqrt{1 + z^2} \qquad R = A/P

solution.title: Flow area
solution.text: Use the trapezoid area formula.

solution.title: Wetted perimeter
solution.text: Each sloping side has length $y\sqrt{1+z^2}$.

solution.title: Hydraulic radius
solution.text: Divide the area by the wetted perimeter.

solution.title: Discharge
solution.text: Apply Manning's equation.

questions.insight: The wetted perimeter uses the true sloping length of the sides; side slopes add area cheaply, which is why trapezoidal canals are so common.
commonErrors: Taking each side length as $zy$ instead of $y\sqrt{1+z^2}$ (equivalently using the top width as the perimeter) gives $9.92\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Using $A = by + zy^2/2$ (only one side triangle) gives $6.55\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
Using $S$ instead of $S^{1/2}$ gives $0.262\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Most efficient rectangular channel section
questions.stem: A rectangular concrete channel ($n = 0.013$) laid on a slope of 0.001 must carry $3.0\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ in uniform flow. If the most efficient (best hydraulic) rectangular section is used, what is the required bottom width?

solution.title: Section properties
solution.text: For the most efficient rectangle the width is twice the depth.

solution.title: Substitute into Manning
solution.text: Collect the powers of $y$.

solution.title: Solve for the depth
solution.text: Isolate $y^{8/3}$.

solution.title: Bottom width
solution.text: Double the depth.

questions.insight: The best hydraulic section minimises wetted perimeter for a given area; for a rectangle that happens when the depth is half the width, so $R = y/2$.
commonErrors: Reporting the depth (0.992 m) instead of the width.
Taking $R = y$ instead of $y/2$ gives a width of 1.668 m.
Assuming a square section ($b = y$) gives 1.424 m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Critical depth in a rectangular channel
questions.stem: A rectangular channel 4.0 m wide carries $12\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$. What is the critical depth? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.

solution.title: Unit discharge
solution.text: Divide the discharge by the width.

solution.title: Critical depth formula
solution.text: Substitute into the rectangular-channel expression.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute.

questions.insight: At critical depth the specific energy is a minimum, $E_c = 1.5y_c = 1.46\text{ m}$, and the Froude number equals 1.
commonErrors: Using $q$ instead of $q^2$ gives 0.674 m.
Using the total discharge $Q$ instead of $q$ gives 2.448 m.
Using $q^2/2g$ inside the cube root gives 0.771 m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Energy loss in a hydraulic jump
questions.stem: Water flows in a 3.0 m wide rectangular channel at $15\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ with a depth of 0.50 m just upstream of a hydraulic jump. Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, determine the head loss across the jump.
questions.required: The head loss $h_L$ across the jump.

variables.meaning: Depths before and after the jump

solution.title: Upstream velocity and Froude number
solution.text: Use $q = Q/b = 5.0\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$.

solution.text: Apply the momentum (Belanger) equation.

solution.title: Head loss
solution.text: Use the closed-form energy loss for a rectangular channel.

solution.title: Check with specific energies
solution.text: Compute $E_1 - E_2$ directly.

questions.insight: A strong jump ($F_1 \approx 4.5$) dissipates almost 45% of the upstream specific energy, which is why jumps are used in stilling basins below spillways.
commonErrors: Using $F_1$ instead of $F_1^2$ in the sequent-depth equation gives $y_2 = 1.273$ m and $h_L = 0.182$ m.
Squaring instead of cubing $(y_2 - y_1)$ gives 1.019 m.
Taking $E_2 = y_2$ (forgetting the downstream velocity head) gives 2.644 m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Liquidity index of a clay from moisture-can data
questions.stem: A clay from a Pampanga borrow pit has a liquid limit of 48% and a plastic limit of 22%. A moisture-content sample of the natural soil has a moist mass of 182.4 g and an oven-dry mass of 139.0 g. What is the liquidity index of the soil in its natural state?
given: Moist mass $= 182.4\text{ g}$, dry mass $= 139.0\text{ g}$

solution.title: Natural water content
solution.text: Water content is based on the dry mass.

solution.title: Plasticity index
solution.text: Range of water contents over which the soil is plastic.

solution.title: Liquidity index
solution.text: Locate the natural water content within the plastic range.

questions.insight: An $LI$ between 0 and 1 means the soil is in the plastic state; values near 0 indicate a stiff, possibly overconsolidated clay.
commonErrors: Computing the consistency index $(LL - w)/PI$ instead gives 0.645.
Computing water content on the moist mass ($w = 23.79\%$) gives $LI = 0.069$.
Inverting the ratio, $PI/(w - PL)$, gives 2.819.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Relative compaction from a sand-cone test
questions.stem: A sand-cone test on a compacted embankment fill gives the following: volume of the test hole $= 950\text{ cm}^3$, mass of moist soil removed $= 1.89\text{ kg}$, and water content $= 11.5\%$. The laboratory standard Proctor test on the same soil gave a maximum dry unit weight of $18.6\text{ kN/m}^3$. Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the relative compaction of the fill?

solution.title: Field moist unit weight
solution.text: Convert the mass to weight and divide by the hole volume.

solution.title: Field dry unit weight
solution.text: Remove the water.

solution.title: Relative compaction
solution.text: Compare with the laboratory maximum.

questions.insight: Many specifications require at least 95% of the standard Proctor maximum for embankments, so this lift would typically need more rolling.
commonErrors: Using the moist unit weight instead of the dry unit weight gives 104.93%.
Inverting the ratio (laboratory over field) gives 106.26%.
Converting $950\text{ cm}^3$ as $0.0095\text{ m}^3$ gives 9.41%.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Relative density of a sand deposit
questions.stem: Laboratory tests on a clean sand give a maximum void ratio of 0.85 and a minimum void ratio of 0.45. The specific gravity of solids is 2.66. In the field, the sand has a dry unit weight of $16.2\text{ kN/m}^3$. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the relative density of the deposit?

formulas.label: Void ratio from dry unit weight

solution.title: Field void ratio
solution.text: From the dry unit weight relation.

solution.title: Relative density formula
solution.text: Measure how far the field state is from the loosest state.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute and express as a percentage.

questions.insight: A relative density of about 60% corresponds to a medium-dense sand; the same formula with unit weights must include the $\gamma_{d,max}/\gamma_d$ factor.
commonErrors: Using $(e - e_{min})/(e_{max} - e_{min})$ gives 40.19%.
Using $\gamma_w = 10\text{ kN/m}^3$ gives 52.01%.
Using $(\gamma_d - \gamma_{d,min})/(\gamma_{d,max} - \gamma_{d,min})$ without the $\gamma_{d,max}/\gamma_d$ factor gives 53.84%.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Hydraulic conductivity from a constant-head test
questions.stem: In a constant-head permeability test, a sand specimen 250 mm long and 100 mm in diameter is subjected to a constant head difference of 600 mm. A volume of $450\text{ cm}^3$ of water is collected in 3 minutes. What is the coefficient of permeability?
questions.required: The coefficient of permeability $k$ in cm/s.

solution.title: Specimen area
solution.text: Work in centimetres.

solution.title: Substitute into Darcy's law
solution.text: Use $L = 25\text{ cm}$, $h = 60\text{ cm}$, $t = 180\text{ s}$.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute.

questions.insight: A value of about $10^{-2}$ cm/s is typical of a clean fine-to-medium sand.
commonErrors: Using the diameter as the radius in the area gives 0.003316 cm/s.
Using the time in minutes instead of seconds gives 0.7958 cm/s.
Interchanging $L$ and $h$ gives 0.07639 cm/s.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Hydraulic conductivity from a falling-head test
questions.stem: A falling-head permeability test is run on a silty clay specimen 15 cm long with a cross-sectional area of $30\text{ cm}^2$. The standpipe has a cross-sectional area of $1.2\text{ cm}^2$. The head in the standpipe drops from 90 cm to 45 cm in 8 minutes. What is the coefficient of permeability, in units of $10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$?

solution.title: Write the falling-head equation
solution.text: It comes from equating the standpipe outflow to the Darcy flow through the specimen and integrating.

solution.title: Convert
solution.text: Divide by 100 to get m/s.

questions.insight: Halving the head always takes the same time in a falling-head test, which is a quick check on laboratory readings.
commonErrors: Using $\log_{10}$ without the factor 2.303 gives $3.76 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s.
Omitting the logarithm entirely gives $12.50 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s.
Treating the test as constant-head with the average head (67.5 cm) gives $8.33 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Daily seepage under a sheet-pile cofferdam from a flow net
questions.stem: A flow net drawn for seepage beneath a sheet-pile wall has 4 flow channels and 12 equipotential drops. The head difference between the upstream and downstream water levels is 6.0 m, and the coefficient of permeability of the sand is $2.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$. What is the total seepage, in cubic metres per day, under a 30 m length of the wall?

formulas.label: Seepage from a flow net (per unit length)

solution.title: Seepage per metre
solution.text: Apply the flow-net equation.

solution.title: Total for 30 m
solution.text: Multiply by the wall length.

solution.title: Convert to per day
solution.text: Multiply by 86 400 s/day.

questions.insight: The flow net ratio $N_f/N_d$ is a shape factor; it does not depend on the head or the permeability, only on the geometry.
commonErrors: Inverting the ratio ($N_d/N_f$) gives $1166.4\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$.
Forgetting to multiply by the wall length gives $4.32\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$.
Multiplying by 3600 instead of 86 400 gives $5.40$, which is the seepage per hour, not per day.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Effective stress under upward seepage
questions.stem: A 2.0 m thick sand layer ($\gamma_{sat} = 19.8\text{ kN/m}^3$) lies at the bottom of an excavation, with water ponded at its top surface. Artesian pressure in an underlying gravel causes water to flow upward through the sand with a total head loss of 1.4 m across the layer. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the vertical effective stress at the bottom of the sand layer?
questions.required: The vertical effective stress $\sigma'$ at the base of the sand.

solution.title: Submerged unit weight
solution.text: Subtract the unit weight of water.

solution.title: Hydraulic gradient
solution.text: Head loss divided by flow length.

solution.title: Effective stress
solution.text: Upward seepage force reduces the effective stress.

questions.insight: The critical gradient is $\gamma'/\gamma_w = 1.02$; at $i = 0.70$ the sand is still stable but carries very little effective stress, so heave is a real risk.
commonErrors: Ignoring the seepage gives 19.98 kPa.
Treating the flow as downward (adding the seepage force) gives 33.71 kPa.
Using $\gamma_{sat}$ instead of $\gamma'$ with the seepage term gives 25.87 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Stress increase below a square footing by the 2:1 method
questions.stem: A 2.0 m by 2.0 m square footing carries a total vertical load of 800 kN. Using the 2:1 (two vertical to one horizontal) load-spread method, estimate the average vertical stress increase at a depth of 3.0 m below the base of the footing.

solution.title: Spread area at depth
solution.text: The load spreads 1 horizontal per 2 vertical on each side, adding $z$ to each dimension.

solution.title: Apply the 2:1 method
solution.text: Divide the load by the spread area.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: Compute.

questions.insight: The contact pressure of 200 kPa has dropped to 16% of its value at a depth of 1.5B; the 2:1 method gives an average, not the peak under the centre.
commonErrors: Adding only $z/2$ to each dimension gives 65.31 kPa.
Adding $2z$ to each dimension gives 12.50 kPa.
Spreading in one direction only, $Q/[(B+z)L]$, gives 80.00 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Boussinesq stress from a point load at an offset
questions.stem: A vertical point load of 500 kN acts on the surface of a deep, homogeneous, elastic soil mass. Using Boussinesq's solution, determine the vertical stress increase at a depth of 4.0 m and a horizontal distance of 3.0 m from the line of action of the load.

solution.title: Stress directly below the load at this depth
solution.text: Evaluate the leading factor.

solution.title: Offset factor
solution.text: With $r/z = 0.75$.

solution.title: Stress increase
solution.text: Divide by the offset factor.

questions.insight: At an offset of 0.75z the stress is only one third of the value on the load axis; point-load stresses decay quickly with lateral distance.
commonErrors: Ignoring the offset (stress on the load axis) gives 14.92 kPa.
Using an exponent of 3/2 instead of 5/2 gives 7.639 kPa.
Using the radial distance $R = \sqrt{r^2 + z^2} = 5\text{ m}$ in place of $z$ in the leading factor gives 3.129 kPa.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Field consolidation time from a laboratory test
questions.stem: A 25 mm thick specimen of clay, drained at both top and bottom in an oedometer, reaches 50% consolidation in 4.5 minutes. The same clay exists in the field as a 5.0 m thick layer drained only at its top (the bottom rests on impervious rock). Assuming the same coefficient of consolidation, how many days will the field layer take to reach 50% consolidation?
given: Lab: thickness $25\text{ mm}$, double drainage, $t_{50} = 4.5\text{ min}$
Same $c_v$ and same degree of consolidation

variables.meaning: Length of the longest drainage path

solution.title: Drainage path lengths
solution.text: Double drainage halves the path; single drainage uses the full thickness.

solution.title: Scale the time
solution.text: Equal $T_v$ and $c_v$ means time varies with the square of the drainage path.

solution.title: Convert to days
solution.text: Divide by 1440 min/day.

questions.insight: Consolidation time grows with the square of the drainage path, so installing sand drains or providing bottom drainage shortens it dramatically.
commonErrors: Using the full 25 mm as the laboratory drainage path (or 2.5 m in the field) gives 125 days.
Forgetting to square the thickness ratio gives 1.25 days.
Making both drainage-path errors gives 31.25 days.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Settlement of an overconsolidated clay crossing its preconsolidation pressure
questions.stem: A 5.0 m thick clay layer lies beneath 3.0 m of sand ($\gamma = 18\text{ kN/m}^3$). The water table is at the top of the clay. The clay has $\gamma_{sat} = 17.8\text{ kN/m}^3$, $e_0 = 0.95$, compression index $C_c = 0.40$, swell (recompression) index $C_s = 0.06$, and preconsolidation pressure $\sigma'_c = 120\text{ kPa}$. A new warehouse floor increases the vertical stress at mid-depth of the clay by 80 kPa. Using the mid-depth stresses and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, estimate the primary consolidation settlement.
given: Water table at the top of the clay

solution.title: Initial effective stress at mid-clay (5.5 m depth)
solution.text: Sand above the water table plus 2.5 m of submerged clay.

solution.title: Compare with the preconsolidation pressure
solution.text: The final stress exceeds $\sigma'_c$, so the stress path crosses from recompression to virgin compression.

solution.title: Recompression part
solution.text: Use $C_s$ from $\sigma'_0$ up to $\sigma'_c$.

solution.title: Virgin compression part
solution.text: Use $C_c$ from $\sigma'_c$ to $\sigma'_f$.

solution.title: Total settlement
solution.text: Add the two parts.

questions.insight: Preconsolidation protects the clay only up to $\sigma'_c$; once the load pushes past it the much larger $C_c$ governs and most of the settlement comes from that branch.
commonErrors: Treating the clay as normally consolidated (using $C_c$ over the whole range) gives 326.53 mm.
Using $C_s$ over the whole range gives 48.98 mm.
Dividing by $e_0$ instead of $1 + e_0$ gives 294.28 mm.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Friction angle from two direct shear tests
questions.stem: Two direct shear tests are performed on specimens of a compacted silty sand in a 60 mm by 60 mm shear box. In the first test, a normal load of 360 N produces failure at a shear load of 270 N. In the second test, a normal load of 720 N produces failure at a shear load of 420 N. Assuming a linear Mohr-Coulomb envelope, what is the angle of internal friction?

variables.meaning: Normal stress on the shear plane

solution.title: Stresses for each test
solution.text: Divide loads by the box area.

solution.title: Slope of the envelope
solution.text: The two failure points define the line.

solution.title: Friction angle
solution.text: Take the inverse tangent.

solution.title: Cohesion intercept (for completeness)
solution.text: Back-substitute either point.

questions.insight: With two tests the envelope has both a slope and an intercept; assuming $c = 0$ from a single test overstates $\phi$ for a soil with cohesion.
commonErrors: Assuming $c = 0$ and using test 1 alone gives $36.87^\circ$.
Assuming $c = 0$ and using test 2 alone gives $30.26^\circ$.
Taking $\sin^{-1}$ of the slope instead of $\tan^{-1}$ gives $24.62^\circ$.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Deviator stress at failure in a drained triaxial test
questions.stem: A soil has effective strength parameters $c' = 12\text{ kPa}$ and $\phi' = 30^\circ$. A consolidated-drained triaxial test is run at an effective cell pressure of 150 kPa. What deviator stress will cause failure?

solution.text: Substitute into the failure relation.

solution.title: Deviator stress
solution.text: Subtract the cell pressure.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Allowable load on a strip footing by Terzaghi
questions.stem: A strip footing 1.5 m wide is founded at a depth of 1.2 m in a soil with $\gamma = 18\text{ kN/m}^3$, $c = 15\text{ kPa}$ and $\phi = 25^\circ$. The water table is very deep. Use Terzaghi's equation for general shear failure, $q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5\gamma BN_\gamma$, with $N_c = 25.13$, $N_q = 12.72$ and $N_\gamma = 8.34$. With a factor of safety of 3 on the ultimate (gross) bearing capacity, what is the allowable load per metre length of footing?

formulas.label: Terzaghi strip footing
formulas.tex: q_u = cN_c + qN_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma BN_\gamma, \qquad q = \gamma D_f

solution.title: Overburden pressure
solution.text: Soil above the footing base.

solution.title: Ultimate bearing capacity
solution.text: Evaluate each term.

solution.title: Allowable pressure
solution.text: Apply the factor of safety.

solution.title: Allowable load per metre
solution.text: Multiply by the footing width.

Forgetting the factor of safety gives 1146.44 kN/m.
Reporting the allowable pressure (254.76 kPa) as the load per metre.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Column load on a square footing with a high water table
questions.stem: A 2.0 m by 2.0 m square footing is founded at a depth of 1.5 m in a sand with $c = 0$ and $\phi = 32^\circ$. The water table is 1.0 m below the ground surface. The sand has $\gamma = 17.5\text{ kN/m}^3$ above the water table and $\gamma_{sat} = 20.0\text{ kN/m}^3$ below it. Use Terzaghi's equation for a square footing, $q_u = 1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.4\gamma BN_\gamma$, with $N_q = 28.52$ and $N_\gamma = 26.87$, and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$. With a factor of safety of 3 on the gross ultimate bearing capacity, what is the maximum allowable column load?

variables.meaning: Effective overburden pressure at footing level
Submerged unit weight below the footing

solution.title: Effective overburden at the footing base
solution.text: 1.0 m of moist sand plus 0.5 m of submerged sand.

solution.title: Unit weight in the $N_\gamma$ term
solution.text: The failure zone below the footing is fully submerged.

solution.title: Ultimate bearing capacity
solution.text: The cohesion term vanishes for $c = 0$.

solution.title: Allowable column load
solution.text: Apply the factor of safety and multiply by the footing area.

questions.insight: A high water table cuts both the overburden and the width terms because effective, not total, unit weights control frictional strength.
commonErrors: Ignoring the water table (moist unit weight everywhere) gives 1499.77 kN.
Using the strip-footing coefficient $0.5$ instead of $0.4$ in the $N_\gamma$ term gives 1224.29 kN.
Forgetting to multiply by the footing area gives 287.82.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Rankine active thrust with a uniform surcharge
questions.stem: A 6.0 m high retaining wall with a smooth vertical back supports a horizontal backfill of dry sand with $\gamma = 18\text{ kN/m}^3$, $c = 0$ and $\phi = 32^\circ$. A uniform surcharge of 15 kPa acts on the backfill surface. Using Rankine's active earth pressure coefficient $K_a = \tan^2(45^\circ - \phi/2)$, determine the total active thrust on the wall per metre length.
given: Smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill, no water

solution.title: Active coefficient
solution.text: Evaluate for $\phi = 32^\circ$.

solution.title: Thrust from the surcharge
solution.text: A uniform surcharge produces a rectangular pressure diagram.

solution.title: Thrust from the soil weight
solution.text: The soil produces a triangular pressure diagram.

solution.title: Total active thrust
solution.text: Add the two components.

questions.insight: The resultant acts about 2.22 m above the base, higher than $H/3$ because the surcharge component acts at mid-height.
commonErrors: Ignoring the surcharge gives 99.55 kN/m.
Using the passive coefficient $K_p = \tan^2(45^\circ + \phi/2)$ gives 1347.40 kN/m.
Omitting the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the triangular component gives 226.76 kN/m.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Allowable capacity of a bored pile in clay
questions.stem: A 400 mm diameter bored concrete pile is installed to a depth of 15 m in a uniform clay with undrained shear strength $c_u = 50\text{ kPa}$. Use an adhesion factor $\alpha = 0.75$ for skin friction and $N_c = 9$ for end bearing ($q_b = 9c_u$). With a factor of safety of 2.5, what is the allowable axial load of the pile?

solution.title: Skin friction
solution.text: Multiply the unit adhesion by the shaft surface area.

solution.title: End bearing
solution.text: Multiply $9c_u$ by the base area.

solution.title: Ultimate capacity
solution.text: Add the components.

solution.title: Allowable load
solution.text: Apply the factor of safety.

questions.insight: In clay most of the capacity of a slender pile comes from the shaft; end bearing here is only about 7% of the total.
commonErrors: Forgetting the factor of safety gives 763.41 kN.
Ignoring end bearing gives 282.74 kN.
Using $\pi D^2$ (no $\tfrac{1}{4}$) for the base area gives 373.22 kN.

questions.subject: hge
questions.title: Infinite slope with seepage parallel to the surface
questions.stem: A long natural slope in Benguet is inclined at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal. A potential slip surface lies parallel to the ground at a vertical depth of 3.0 m. During the rainy season the water table rises to the ground surface and seepage is parallel to the slope. The soil has $c' = 8\text{ kPa}$, $\phi' = 30^\circ$ and $\gamma_{sat} = 19.5\text{ kN/m}^3$. Using the infinite-slope method and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the factor of safety against sliding?
given: Vertical depth to slip surface $H = 3.0\text{ m}$
Water table at the surface, seepage parallel to the slope

formulas.label: Infinite slope, seepage parallel to slope

variables.meaning: Vertical depth to the slip surface

solution.title: Trigonometric terms
solution.text: Evaluate for $\beta = 25^\circ$.

solution.title: Cohesion term
solution.text: Divide $c'$ by the driving shear stress per unit area.

solution.title: Friction term
solution.text: Pore pressure from parallel seepage leaves only $\gamma'$ effective on the slip plane.

solution.title: Factor of safety
solution.text: Add the two terms.

questions.insight: With $FS < 1$ the slope is predicted to fail when fully saturated; seepage roughly halves the frictional resistance, which is why rain-induced landslides are common on Philippine mountain slopes.
commonErrors: Ignoring pore pressure (using $\tan\phi'/\tan\beta$ without the $\gamma'/\gamma_{sat}$ factor) gives 1.595.
Ignoring cohesion gives 0.615.
Using $\gamma'$ instead of $\gamma_{sat}$ in the cohesion term gives 1.334.
